Upon emergence, the newly hatched chicks display a wet birth mass averaging 38.5 grams [Wwb = 38.5 grams], a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves allocated to the semi-precocial offspring of this species. This initial mass is relatively modest compared to the ultimate adult body sizes observed in the population, highlighting the rapid growth phase that must ensue. The reproductive strategy of Larus delawarensis involves a single annual clutch, with females on average producing a clutch of three eggs per nest [N_R_i = three eggs per nest] and raising only one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year], corresponding to an annual output of approximately 3 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 3 eggs per year] at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This moderate reproductive output is characteristic of many large gulls, balancing the energetic demands of incubation and extended parental care against the need for chick survival in variable coastal environments.

This impressive lifespan is among the longer reported for gulls of similar body mass and is likely facilitated by a relatively low adult mortality rate once the challenging juvenile and sub-adult years are past. This size difference between the sexes is an important factor in their respective foraging strategies and competitive interactions during the breeding season.

From a comparative perspective, the life-history strategy of the Ring-billed gull is one of a slow pace of life, characterized by a delayed first reproduction and a long potential lifespan. The time since birth at first brood, estimated at 730 days [tR = 730 days] under typical adult thermal regimes of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], is a period largely spent in the immature and subadult stages, during which the young birds refine their foraging skills and establish territories for future nesting.
